note: Which dashes on the pattern-to-product index (map/stack.html) are verdicts rather than gaps. The single source: tools/src/lib/site-map.ts (buildStack) reads it at site build. `bands` maps a pattern band's area id to the note printed under its heading, saying why no pattern in it is for sale; `patterns` maps one pattern's slug, outside those bands, to the one-line reason no cloud sells it, printed under the pattern's name. A pattern either is for sale — an implements edge from a capability in relations.json — or is listed here, or is a gap still to map: the build refuses an entry a capability contradicts, a pattern its band already covers, and a band or pattern the index does not hold.

bands.gof: None of these is a service. They live inside one process, so every dash below is the right answer rather than a missing mapping.
bands.ddd: These are modelling decisions in your own code. Nothing in this section is purchasable, and nothing should be.
bands.functional: These are language and composition techniques. There is no product column to fill.
bands.testing: Test doubles live in your test suite. A managed service cannot stand in for one, so every row is dashed by nature.
bands.frontend: These structure code that runs in the browser. Hosting is buyable; the structure is not.
bands.enterprise: These organise one application's own business logic and data access. A framework or an ORM may ship them; no cloud rents them as a service.

patterns.acp: A protocol between an editor and a coding agent, run locally; there is no hosted service to rent.
patterns.active-object: A concurrency structure inside one process.
patterns.api-versioning: A contract decision in your own API; a gateway can route versions but cannot design them.
patterns.backpressure: Flow control between your own producer and consumer.
patterns.barrier: A synchronisation primitive inside one process.
patterns.bff: An API you write per client; an API gateway can host it but does not make it.
patterns.bulkhead: Pool and partition sizes you set in your own process or deployment.
patterns.client-side-cache: Lives in the caller: a browser, an SDK or an HTTP client.
patterns.consistent-hashing: Runs inside the partitioner of a store or a load balancer; you buy the store, not the ring.
patterns.containerization: Packaging you do; compute demands it, and sells the registry and the image build around it.
patterns.context-engineering: A discipline in how you assemble each model call.
patterns.copy-on-write: A memory technique inside one process or file system.
patterns.count-min-sketch: A data structure you embed in your own code or stream job.
patterns.cqrs: A split you design between your own write model and read model; the stores on each side are bought separately.
patterns.crdt: A data type you build replication on; only Azure Managed Redis active geo-replication uses CRDTs underneath, and it sells the replication, not the type.
patterns.double-checked-locking: An initialisation idiom inside one process.
patterns.event-carried-state-transfer: A decision about what your own events carry.
patterns.fallback: A decision in the caller's code about what to answer when a dependency fails.
patterns.fan-in: A merge your own consumer performs.
patterns.fencing-token: A number your storage layer must check on every write; no service checks it for you.
patterns.fork-join: A parallel-execution construct inside one process.
patterns.functional-partitioning: A decision about which data lives in which of your stores.
patterns.generalization: A property of the model you train, not a service.
patterns.geohash: An encoding you compute; stores that index locations use it inside.
patterns.gossip-protocol: A protocol inside a cluster's membership layer.
patterns.heartbeat: A liveness signal your own processes send and check.
patterns.hedged-request: A client-side policy: send a second copy after a delay and take the first answer.
patterns.hexagonal: A boundary you draw in your own code between the core and its adapters.
patterns.idempotency: A key your own handler records and checks; broker-side de-duplication only narrows the window.
patterns.inbox: A table your consumer writes in the same transaction as its effect.
patterns.layered: A way to arrange your own code into tiers; every host runs it.
patterns.least-privilege: A discipline in how you grant access; IAM Access Analyzer and IAM Recommender report what you granted too broadly.
patterns.load-shedding: A server's own decision, under overload, to refuse work it cannot finish in time.
patterns.long-polling: A request your client holds open; Amazon SQS's receive wait time is one product that offers it as an option.
patterns.merkle-tree: A data structure inside replication and sync protocols.
patterns.microkernel: A plugin seam you design into your own application.
patterns.microservices: A decomposition decision; the containers, queues and gateways it runs on are each mapped on their own rows.
patterns.monitor-object: A synchronisation construct inside one process.
patterns.mvc: A structure inside one application's code.
patterns.mvp: A structure inside one application's code.
patterns.mvvm: A structure inside one application's code.
patterns.pagination: A contract in your own API.
patterns.pessimistic-locking: A lock your database takes inside a transaction (SELECT … FOR UPDATE).
patterns.priority-queue: No managed queue on the three clouds orders messages by priority; a queue per priority is the usual answer, or RabbitMQ priority queues.
patterns.proactor: An asynchronous I/O loop inside one process.
patterns.reactor: An event loop inside one process.
patterns.refresh-ahead: No managed cache refreshes entries before they expire; the timer and the reload are yours.
patterns.repr: A way to shape your own endpoints; any web framework hosts it.
patterns.ring-buffer: A data structure inside one process.
patterns.semaphore: A synchronisation primitive inside one process.
patterns.server-sent-events: An HTTP response your own server streams; every host that keeps a connection open can serve it.
patterns.sliding-window: A counting technique you write into your own limiter or stream job.
patterns.stateless-service: A discipline elastic compute demands of you rather than sells: keep no state in the instance.
patterns.thread-confinement: A discipline in your own code.
patterns.trie: A data structure inside your own code.
patterns.two-phase-commit: Runs inside a database or a transaction manager; no cloud sells it across services.
patterns.unique-id-generation: A scheme you run in your own services; databases offer sequences, not a global ID service.
patterns.vector-clock: Metadata inside a replicated store's protocol.
patterns.vertical-partitioning: A schema decision in your own data model.
patterns.vertical-slice: A way to cut your own codebase by feature; nothing to rent.
patterns.web-queue-worker: An arrangement of a web tier, a queue and workers, each bought separately and mapped on its own row.
patterns.write-ahead-log: Runs inside every database engine; point-in-time restore is what it buys you, and that is sold on the databases page.
patterns.write-behind: No managed cache writes back to your database for you; the queue and the flush are yours.
